comments.author: @giannisolga5191
comments.text: Congratulations on this wonderful video. I once worked in Khamis Mushayt in Saudi Arabia. The distant plain was a light coloured stony desert in which a single black mountain stood out strikingly. It was called Queen of Sheba Mountain (Jabal Maliqat Saba’). It was a way station on the Frankincense Road from Dhauka and Shisa in Oman. The caravans came up from Najran (Ukhdood). We climbed the black mountain. There was an engraved stone image of a goddess, and an inscription. Cambridge University said it was Himyaritic. We visited Najran and were permitted to view the archaeologic site of Ukhdood, where there was a temple and Sabaean and Himyaritic inscriptions. Frankincense and myrrh were sold in the local beduin market, for dental hygiene and toothache. So to see in your video Boswellia sacra, whose resin gives frankincense, at the source in Dhauka and Shisa in Dhofar was absolutely thrilling!. Thank you!!! In Cyprus I encountered an Englishman who had flown a helicopter in Dhofar in the employ of Sultan Qaboos during the campaign against the Marxist insurgents from South Yemen. In a canyon his machine lost lift and crashed, causing back injury. He had a gold neckchain, bracelet and ring and said the Sultan paid well. I didn’t know that the Omani Sultanate split into the Zanzibari and Omani sultanates. That later the Arabian part split again into the Salalah and Musqat entities. I was saddened by the death of Sultan Qaboos. I hope Oman continues his legacy as a peacemaker in these troubled times. Thank you for this interesting information and for the fantastic video.

replies.author: @WhereonEarth4K
replies.text: That's an extraordinary set of firsthand memories - climbing the black mountain to find a Himyaritic goddess inscription, then later meeting someone who'd flown missions in Dhofar itself. The frankincense connection landing all the way back to Boswellia sacra at its actual source must have been a genuinely thrilling full-circle moment. Thank you for such a rich addition, and glad the video could honor Sultan Qaboos's legacy the way it seems to have.
